title: TeamPCP
summary: TeamPCP, also tracked publicly as PCPCat, ShellForce, DeadCatx3, SHADOW-WATER-058 and UNC6780, is a financially motivated intrusion set whose documented activity centres on cloud-native and containerised environments rather than on end-user laptops. Public reporting describes large-scale internet scanning for exposed services, followed by abuse of misconfigured authentication to plant tooling inside running containers and to steal credentials, keys and tokens from environment variables, mounted secrets and configuration files. The group's name in one earlier reporting thread referenced its use of a self-propagating shell script that spread from one exposed host to others, which is why mass scanning and rapid reuse of stolen keys are core behaviours to hunt for. Reported monetisation belongs to the opportunistic end of the market: cryptocurrency mining, resale of access, and in some campaigns extortion or ransomware staging. Evidence of these intrusions appears in container runtime logs, sudden container creation, unexpected outbound mining traffic, new scheduled tasks, edited shell startup files and new authorised keys on Linux hosts.

beginner.definition: TeamPCP is a criminal group that attacks cloud servers and containers instead of office laptops. Security companies also call it PCPCat, ShellForce and UNC6780. It looks for servers that are open to the internet with weak or missing passwords. Then it steals keys, runs hidden software and spreads to more servers.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modern companies run much of their work in containers and cloud accounts. Those systems often hold powerful keys that open many doors at once. If an attacker steals one key, they may reach the whole cloud account. Because containers are replaced often, the damage can be hidden inside a system that looks healthy and busy.
howItWorks: The group scans the whole internet for cloud services left open by mistake.
It tries default or empty passwords, and gets in without any exploit.
Inside a container, it reads keys and passwords stored in settings.
It runs a hidden mining or proxy program using the victim's computer power.
It uses the stolen keys to reach other servers and repeats the process.
It adds scheduled jobs and login keys so it can return later.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats where every door has the same simple lock, and some doors are not locked at all. A thief walks the corridor, tries one key on every door, and gets into many homes in a single evening. Then they copy any spare keys they find on the kitchen table and use them in the next building. Scanning exposed cloud services works in exactly this way.
takeaways: A cloud service should never be reachable from the internet without authentication.
Secrets stored in container settings are readable by anything running inside it; use a proper secret store.
Unexpected mining traffic or new login keys on a server are strong signs of this kind of intrusion.

objectives: Explain why exposed cloud services are the preferred entry point for TeamPCP-style intrusions.
Describe how stolen API keys and tokens turn one compromised host into many.
Recognise evidence of cryptomining and persistence inside a container environment.
List the configuration checks that remove anonymous access to cloud services.
Explain how to rotate credentials safely after exposure of a secret.
Compare the risks of container workloads with those of traditional server workloads.
